::: {.lede}
I study how claims that begin outside legitimate institutions end up inside them: which conspiratorial allegations circulating on fringe platforms get taken up by American political elites, what happens to those allegations along the way, and whether the public treats a claim differently depending on where it is said to have come from.
:::

The working hypothesis is that allegations are **laundered** in transit. A claim leaves an imageboard carrying a stigma. Somewhere between there and a debate stage the stigma comes off: the wording is recoded, the messenger changes, and the named source is replaced with *people are saying*. By the time an officeholder repeats it, it is no longer a fringe claim with a traceable origin; it is a constituent concern. I treat laundering as a mechanism to be tested, not a label, and I build the evidence so it can fail.
